analysis.one_liner: Restricts payday-style small-dollar lenders, blocks predatory payment withdrawals, and bans overdraft fees on prepaid accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2025 with 3 cosponsors and has sat in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Lending Act targets common practices in small-dollar online lending. It would stop companies from pulling money out of your bank account through checks you never authorized, give you the right to stop automatic payments to a lender, require payday and other small-dollar lenders to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, force online lenders to follow the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, ban overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, and shut down data brokers who sell borrowers' bank information to payday lenders. It has not moved since being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday loans, installment loans, and prepaid debit accounts — typically lower-income households facing short-term cash gaps. They gain control over who can take money from their accounts, protection from lenders charging interest rates their own state has outlawed, and fewer surprise fees on prepaid cards. All consumers gain from limits on unauthorized 'remotely created checks' that drain bank accounts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday borrowers and prepaid card users

how_it_helps.text: Remotely created checks — checks that can debit your account without your signature — could only be issued by a company you named in writing with your bank, and you could revoke that permission at any time.
If you agree to repay a small-dollar loan by electronic transfer, the transfer is treated as a preauthorized transfer, which carries protections including the right to stop payment.

All small-dollar lenders (loans up to $5,000, adjusted for inflation) would have to register with the CFPB before making loans, and any online or bank-issued small-dollar loan would have to comply with the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts would be banned, and companies that collect and sell borrowers' sensitive bank information without directly making the loan would be prohibited from doing so.

analysis.who_pays: Small-dollar lenders such as payday and online installment lenders lose the ability to charge rates and fees barred in the borrower's home state and face a federal registration requirement. Lead generators and data brokers lose the business of collecting and selling borrowers' bank account details to lenders. Banks lose overdraft fee income on prepaid accounts and face tighter limits on processing unauthorized checks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, data brokers, prepaid card issuers

drawbacks.text: Stricter underwriting and state rate caps could shrink access to short-term credit for some borrowers; people who rely on payday loans when other options are unavailable might find fewer lenders willing to serve them.

The bill directs a Government Accountability Office study of capital availability on tribal reservations, an acknowledgment that cracking down on online tribal-affiliated lending raises questions about economic opportunity in Indian Country that the bill addresses by study rather than by policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most borrowers the protections outweigh the cost: the bill's core provisions stop unauthorized account withdrawals and let state rate caps apply to online loans, which address documented harms of high-cost small-dollar lending. The main cost is that some borrowers with poor credit could lose access to the high-priced credit they currently use, which is a real tradeoff but one the bill partially addresses with a study of alternative capital sources on tribal lands.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2025, by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici with Reps. Jayapal and Schakowsky as cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
Its only action since referral is sitting with the committee; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
Three of 217 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans have.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday-style lenders, data brokers, and prepaid card issuers, who face no new rules while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member

for.name: Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jan Schakowsky

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in February 2025 and has not scheduled a hearing or markup since.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the sponsor and all three cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits with a committee chaired by Republicans, so the partisan shape is suggestive but untested.

industries.note: Lenders making loans up to $5,000 would have to register with the CFPB and obey the rate and fee laws of the borrower's state, ending the practice of using federal preemption or offshore setups to charge rates states have banned. Their business depends on high-cost loans to cash-strapped borrowers.

industries.industry: Lead generators and financial data brokers
industries.note: The bill bans gathering or brokering borrowers' sensitive bank information for small-dollar loans unless the broker is directly making the loan, cutting off a profitable funnel that sells payday applicants' details to lenders.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts — used heavily by unbanked and lower-income consumers — would be prohibited, removing a fee stream charged to the accounts least able to absorb it.

Banks would face new duties: honoring written designations for remotely created checks and processing stop-payment rights, and losing overdraft fee income on prepaid accounts. But they also gain certainty that payments they process were consumer-authorized.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup more than halfway through the first session and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very likely to die in the Financial Services Committee this Congress, as similar small-dollar lending bills have in prior sessions.
